---
title: "Delineating potential DRT operating areas: an origin-destination clustering approach"
#author: "Hussein Mahfouz"
abstract: "Investment in Demand-Responsive Transport (DRT) has emerged as a sustainable transport intervention option for areas that are traditionally hard to serve by high frequency public transport. The integration of DRT with public transport could help reduce car mode share, but planning DRT remains challenging; many studies show that DRT can inadvertently reduce public transport demand while also increasing congestion and vehicle-miles travelled (VMT).  More research is needed on how to identify the most viable operating areas of DRT based on the unique demand patterns of an area. This paper investigates delineating service areas of DRT using spatial clustering of spatial flow data. Methods for clustering Origin-Destination (OD) flows are developed to analyse travel patterns in the city of Leeds, UK. We consider clusters based on (a) OD pairs with poor public transport supply, and (b) OD pairs with poor public transport supply and low potential demand. The method identifies clusters of OD flows where latent demand is concentrated, highlighting potential operating areas that are likely to be most effective. The results address one of the main reasons for high DRT failure rates --- unnecessarily flexible ‘many-to-many’ services --- by constraining the service to clusters with poor public transport supply, providing a useful input into additional work. The results provide valuable inputs for visualisations to inform decision-making processes and  models to refine DRT investment plans. The OD clustering approach presented in this paper provides a foundation for agent-based models of DRT and future research into and practical applications of DRT integration with existing public transport systems"

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Bus networks form the backbone of many public transport systems across the world. They offer affordable mobility (an aspect that is important for social inclusion), mitigate congestion, and reduce emissions associated with car dependence. In many cities, bus services have grown gradually to meet increasing demand from the expanding urban core and peripheries, but the quality of service can suffer from issues such as poor access between neighborhoods, inefficient network layouts and poor route synchronization [@ruiz2017improving]. Existing research has been conducted on strategic and tactical redesign of bus networks to increase their attractiveness [@kepaptsoglou2009transit; @ibarra2015planning; @liu2021review]. However, advanced optimisation approaches cannot compensate for the fact that traditional bus services are most suited to dense areas with consistently high demand [@errico2013survey] and are inefficient for suburban areas, villages, and low demand interurban areas [@papanikolaou2017methodological].

Flexible mobility services, such as Demand Responsive Transport (DRT), have been proposed to serve such areas. We follow @davison2014survey in defining DRT: a service that is (a) available to the general public, (b) provided by low capacity vehicles (relative to buses), (c) responsive to changes in demand, and (d) has a fare that is charged per passenger, not per vehicle. While DRT systems have a higher fixed cost per passenger than traditional fixed bus routes [@currie2020most], they aim to compensate for this by reducing operating costs through higher passenger load factors with minimal increase to service distance due to route circuity [@ryley2014investigating]. This balance is difficult to achieve, and even now as technological improvements drive the re-emergence of DRT, failure rates are high and strongly correlated with operating costs [@currie2020most].

<!--# Bus operating costs are driven by the labour costs of the drivers and the distances travelled by the vehicle. Flexible services may have higher operational costs than conventional bus services if they travel further by deviating from a straight route. However, compared to the running of empty buses, flexible services can save kilometre-based costs by not operating unless there is a passenger, even if the labour cost is still incurred. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08111146.2012.660872 -->

Extensive research has been done on DRT planning, but the focus is more on the tactical and operational level and less on the strategic level [@papanikolaou2017methodological]. Strategic level methods that help identify potential DRT operating zones are important given that one of the main determinants of success for a DRT scheme is its ability to concentrate demand geographically and temporally [@enoch2006demand]. Previous work has used accessibility scores to identify potential DRT service areas [@giuffrida2021addressing; @rath2023assessing], but this approach only looks at supply without factoring in travel demand.

This study makes both conceptual and methodological contributions to the strategic level planning of DRT services. Conceptually, it fills an important gap in strategic DRT planning by addressing an unexplored area: the identification of clusters in origin-destination (OD) flows and their implications for DRT service operating areas. This conceptual advancement provides a new perspective on how to approach DRT planning at a strategic level. Methodologically, the study introduces a spatial statistical approach to cluster spatial flow data [@tao2016spatial], and combines it with an assessment of transport supply and demand to identify areas with concentrated travel demand suitable for DRT services. This framework ensures that DRT is not proposed in areas (a) where there is no concentrated demand, and (b) where an improved bus service would be more appropriate. While methods for spatial clustering of flow data are heavily studied in spatial data mining, to our knowledge this is the first paper employing them for strategic DRT planning.

# Literature Review {#sec-lit-review}

<!--# It can be distinguished from traditional fixed route services through: (a) network typology and operation, (b) boarding and alighting locations, (c) schedule, and (d) advanced notice requirement [@papanikolaou2017methodological] -->

<!--# The concept of DRT goes back to the 1970s, and it has taken other names such as Dial-a-Bus, or more recently, micro-transit [@currie2020most]. It is seen as a compromise between the convenience (instant frequency and full coverage) of the automobile, and the cost-effectiveness of public transport [@currie2020most]. Useful diagrams have been made to compare DRT to other travel modes in terms of trade-offs in service frequency --- coverage [@d1994demand] and flexibility --- sustainability [@inturri2019multi]. -->

The term DRT has become an umbrella term for flexible public transport. Services can be grouped under different DRT typologies [@enoch2004intermode] or scheduling and operational characteristics [@d1994demand]. For diagrammatic descriptions of the different operational characteristics, the reader is referred to @mageean2003evaluation and @pavanini2023role.

The wide range of different service offerings and associated investment and planning options highlights the complexity of DRT planning. On the one hand, this flexibility allows DRT services to be tailored to the specific demand patterns of an area. Conversely, the overly complex services, or services that don't match the needs of the local community, are prone to failure [@enoch2006demand]. Choosing the wrong service could lead to bad user experience and unnecessarily expensive operating costs.

## Planning DRT systems {#sec-planning_drt}

The planning of public transport systems with conventional bus services is well established and follows a sequential approach [@ceder1986bus; @ibarra2015planning] that includes *strategic*, *tactical*, and *operational* planning. The high failure rate of DRT systems is related to the lack of a similar robust methodological planning framework for its appraisal [@papanikolaou2017methodological].

In trying to map DRT research onto these planning pillars, @papanikolaou2017methodological find that DRT research can be split into:

1.  Strategic level (economic and econometric studies) studies on DRT area selection and investment evaluations. This includes (a) Research outlining the potential market and operating model of DRT systems [@mulley2009flexible], and (b) Research that compares cost functions of DRT and public transport using analytical methods [@nourbakhsh2012structured].

2.  Tactical and operational level (operations research) studies on system typology definition and operational characteristics (@vansteenwegen2022survey provide a review of this sub-field of the literature).

Whereas the latter is studied extensively, there remains a need to develop general approaches on identifying potential areas for DRT services [@papanikolaou2017methodological]. This has become more necessary as DRT systems evolve from being targeted at special groups (in parallel to conventional public transport), to being integrated with public transport with the aim of improving accessibility for entire communities [@nelson2010recent]. <!--# this should be grounded in accessibility, not something else … cite Tools of the Trade -->

## Existing approaches to DRT service area delineation {#sec-lit-service-areas}

**Analytical models** help decide whether areas should be served by fixed or dynamic (bus or DRT) systems. These models are mostly based on idealized representations at the route level with pre-defined service areas [@quadrifoglio2009methodology; @li2010feeder; @sivakumaran2012cost]. @liu2021mobility propose a modelling framework that treats DRT zone size as a variable to be optimised, along with spacing and headway of the public transport network. The framework, however is based on an idealized grid network with homogeneous travel demand, so cannot easily be extended to real world study areas. @wang2018optimization apply a similar model to define zoning of a many to one DRT service for a terminal in Northwest Calgary, Canada. Even though the approach is applied to a real area, it also uses homogeneous travel demand within zones and is focused on serving one terminal. Our interest is in a preliminary step to identify areas where a DRT service can be a beneficial addition. 

**Accessibility based approaches** help delineate DRT service areas in real city-level case studies. Some studies have restricted DRT services to areas with low public transport accessibility, thereby addressing gaps in the transport network [@giuffrida2021addressing; @rath2023assessing]. Others have focused on providing DRT within buffer zones around rail stations, positioning DRT as a feeder service to enhance rail accessibility (Oke et al., 2020) [@oke2020evaluating].

The DRT investment options are then evaluated using either measures of social equity [@giuffrida2021addressing], or through agent-based simulations [@rath2023assessing; @oke2020evaluating]. While these simulations show that constraining DRT to certain areas can mitigate against undesired mode shift, they are lacking in two aspects. First, travel demand is not factored into the initial zonal configuration, but is only used later to evaluate the network performance. The high variance in mode share results indicate that generic rules based on accessibility levels cannot be applied to all cities, but that specific characteristics of travel demand need to be accounted for when defining operating zones. Secondly, the public transport network is taken as a fixed constraint, and no attempt is made to reconfigure the network.

**Network reconfiguration** approaches have also been used to help delineate DRT service zones. @giuffrida2021addressing simulate network modifications by reassigning vehicles to improve service frequency on routes connecting to railway stations. They then add DRT stops to areas with poor public transport accessibility. While this approach factors in demand conceptually, it does not incorporate a structured approach to delineate zones based on actual demand data. @shen2018integrating adopt a similar approach but use demand data and opt to keep the busiest 90% of routes, replacing the remaining 10% with a flexible service.

Similarly, optimisation algorithms have been developed to algorithmically determine how to edit public transport routes and where to added DRT. @pinto2020joint formulate an optimization problem that minimizes passenger wait time by editing route frequencies, removing routes, and changing DRT fleet size. While this approach uses travel demand to inform where to add DRT stops, it does not limit service areas, allowing DRT fleets to operate across an entire area. This is not ideal as simulation results have shown that competition with public transport, as well as increases in congestion and system-wide total VMT are likely when services are not constrained [@oke2020evaluating; @kagho2021demand; @rath2023assessing]. @zhao2021joint formulate a similar optimisation problem that aims to minimize both travel time and fleet size of public transport and DRT by shortening bus routes and adjusting DRT service areas, though their work is applied to a model network with 5 bus lines.

These optimization models start with an existing public transport network and focus on incremental adjustments—modifying routes, frequencies, or fleet sizes—rather than designing an integrated public transport + DRT network from scratch. While this approach aligns with practical constraints, as major overhauls of bus networks are rare, they may limit the scope of DRT to the edges of the existing network [@zhao2021joint]. However, DRT services could connect people to different stops along a bus route, not just at the edges.

To ensure DRT service areas are optimally located, it is important to base them on spatial and temporal demand patterns [@kagho2021demand], rather than being constrained by the edges of the terminals of the existing bus routes. A method to delineate service areas based on spatial concentrations of travel demand could be useful in two ways: (a) as a simpler alternative to current optimisation-based approaches, addressing root causes of high DRT failure rates identified in the literature, or (b) as a way to generate preliminary DRT zones that serve as inputs for optimization models. Starting with DRT zones informed by actual demand may lead to more effective network configurations compared to models that begin without predefined DRT zones.

The following section examines clustering techniques for identifying these demand concentrations directly from OD data, offering a data-driven foundation for DRT zone delineation.

## **Clustering techniques for identifying demand concentrations in travel patterns**

The approaches outlined in the previous section face limitations, particularly in their poor integration of actual demand data at the strategic level of DRT planning. These limitations can be addressed through methods that capture spatial concentrations in travel demand more effectively.

Clustering methods offer a more precise way to capture concentrated demand patterns that are critical for DRT zone delineation. By analysing OD flow data, clustering can reveal where travel demand is naturally concentrated, helping planners define DRT service areas based on actual demand in real-world study areas. We focus on clustering as standard methods for visualising OD data struggle to capture spatial and temporal variations in demand due to the volume of data being represented [@guo2009flow]. Alternative methods such as community detection [@guo2009flow] and edge bundling methods [@selassie2011divided] have been proposed to mitigate against visual clutter and salience bias. However, these techniques come at the expense of spatial information: community detection reduces spatial granularity, while edge bundling obscures distinct OD patterns in OD data. Since both factors are crucial for our analysis, we rely on clustering methods, which identify patterns directly from raw OD data without altering its spatial characteristics.

<!--# check "An OD clustering method based on vector constraints:  2.1: Visuaising OD flow-->

<!--# from: Detecting arbitrarily shaped clusters in origin-destinatin flows using ant colony optimisation -->

Clustering has emerged as an effective approach for identifying spatial patterns in OD data. Clustering methods can be broadly categorized into two groups [@song2019detecting]: (1) spatial statistics-based methods and (2) hierarchical and density-based clustering methods. The former rely on anomaly detection techniques (based on tests of spatial homogeneity), such as Moran's I, Getis-Ord G, and Ripley's K, extending them from point data to OD data. While these methods detect clusters at different spatial scales, they do not group the data into distinct clusters. In contrast, hierarchical and density-based methods group OD flows based on distance measures, offering more actionable insights for DRT planning.

Density-based clustering is an effective technique for discovering precise clusters in space. DBSCAN (*Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise)* [@ester1996density] is a widely used algorithm, along with its variations like DBSCAN (Hierarchical DBSCAN) [@campello2013density] and OPTICS (*Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure*) [@ankerst1999optics] are also commonly used. These algorithms rely on distances between observations, a metric that is easy to calculate for point data, but less intuitive for other geometries such as lines due to the multilocation nature of each geometry. To address this, @tao2016spatial devise measures to calculate distance between lines, enabling the application of these algorithms to flow data [@tao2016dbscan; @tao2017flowhdbscan; @fang2021adaptive]. Additionally, different approaches have been proposed for incorporating a temporal dimension to the cluster detection [@yao2018stepwise].

The ability of these algorithms to cluster OD 'flow' data without loss of spatial information is invaluable for understanding the spatial concentrations of demand that exist in a network. This research makes use of density-based clustering as part of a larger approach to identify concentrations in travel demand that could be served by DRT.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

DRT services are most effective when aligned with actual travel demand [@dft2020regulatory]. However, there is no standardized method for identifying demand gaps suitable for DRT in a way that ensures seamless integration with existing public transport networks. This section presents a novel approach to address this gap by identifying areas of unmet demand and clustering them to inform potential DRT operating zones. <!--# Could replace second line with: While analytical methods exist for identifying demand gaps on specific routes, there is no standardized approach for city-wide applications in real-world study areas that ensures seamless integration with existing public transport networks.-->

Our method involves two key steps: (1) identifying demand gaps through a supply-demand analysis, and (2) clustering travel demand within these gaps to delineate DRT service areas. First, we define and measure public transport supply (@sec-method-transport-supply) and potential demand (@sec-method-transport-demand) to identify areas with inadequate service. Next, we introduce a clustering approach (@sec-method-clustering-flow-data) to reveal spatial concentrations of travel demand. This clustering is applied to two datasets prepared using the methods in @sec-methods-preparing-data: (1) OD pairs with poor public transport supply, and (2) OD pairs with both poor public transport supply and low potential demand.

The overall workflow is illustrated in @fig-workflow. Our approach is applied to a case study city, Leeds (@sec-case-study), to demonstrate its practical utility.

![Workflow for generating potential DRT zones. The workflow is split into 3 separate steps, and the analysis components of each step are given alphabetical labels to show the order they are carried out in.](images/figure_entire_workflow_3.png){#fig-workflow}

## Case Study {#sec-case-study}

This research uses Leeds, UK, as a case study. As one of the largest European cities without rapid transit, Leeds relies heavily on buses (@fig-rural-urban). The regional transport authority, West Yorkshire Combined Authority (WYCA), has set a net-zero target for 2038, requiring a 52% increase in bus mode share [@wyca2021connectivity] —an ambitious goal given the 15% decline in annual bus trips from 2009 to 2019 [@wyca2021improvement].

Under the Bus Services Act [@uk2017busact], WYCA’s Bus Service Improvement Plan aims to enhance bus services and better integrate multimodal transport [@wyca2021improvement]. DRT is considered a means to improve access in low-density areas, and a pilot service (Flexibus) was trialed in East Leeds. However, during its 18-month pilot phase, it struggled with low ridership, covering only 5% of operating costs [@wyca2022drtflexibusreview]. Its average of 1.38 passengers per trip reflected a service design that failed to effectively pool demand. Services that are informed by spatial concentrations in travel demand could improve DRT viability.

![Urban Rural Classification: Explained in the 2011 Rural-Urban Classification User Guide](images/rural_urban_bus.png){#fig-rural-urban fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Demand data {#sec-methods-preparing-data}

We use trip records for 2019 derived from mobile phone data. The data is provided by Connected Places Catapult[^1] and covers all motorised road and rail trips throughout Great Britain (see @franco2020demand for a description of the data preparation). A data request includes a date range, and a zoning system with zones being individual or groups of MSOAs (there is a cap on the number of zones permitted). The output is the average number of trips between each unique zone pair, disaggregated by hour of day and weekday / weekend. We aggregate the data into five periods (5am - 8am, 8am-11am, 11am-2pm, 2pm-5pm, 5pm-8pm) to simplify the analysis. The methods proposed, however, can be applied at any temporal aggregation.

[^1]: <https://cp.catapult.org.uk/project/great-britain-trip-database-portal/>

### Disaggregating OD data

Our OD data is aggregated at the Middle Super Output Area (MSOA) level, a geographical unit defined by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) that represents areas with populations of 5,000–15,000 people. Our study area, Leeds, is divided into 107 MSOAs. However, this aggregation level is too coarse for our clustering analysis. To address this, we apply jittering [@lovelace2022jittering] to disaggregate OD pairs with high traveller counts into multiple smaller OD pairs. The start and end points of the new ODs are constrained to their original MSOAs, but are snapped probabilistically to subzones of $100m^2$ based on the population density distribution within each MSOA. A disaggregation threshold ensures no OD pair exceeds 100 people.

## Preparing input data for clustering

After disaggregating the OD trip data, we need to decide which OD pairs to use for clustering. If we were to pass all OD pairs to the algorithm, then our clusters may include noise from OD pairs that are well served by public transport. We would also generate DRT zones that serve all demand, whereas our objective is to propose DRT zones that complement bus routes and fill the gaps in the bus network, as explained in @sec-lit-service-areas. We identify gaps in public transport service provision by trying two different inputs: (1) OD pairs with poor public transport supply ($OD_s$) , and (2) OD pairs with poor public transport supply and low potential demand ($OD_{sd}$).

$OD_s$ is meant to suggest DRT zones that complement the existing bus network by only including the OD demand that is not well served by said network, as explained in @sec-method-transport-supply. $OD_{sd}$ is similar, but also excludes OD pairs that could be served by a better bus service. This exclusion is based on criteria explained in @sec-method-transport-demand. The workflow for the supply and demand analysis is shown in @fig-flowchart-scenarios. The number of OD pairs in each approach is shown in @tbl-od_pairs_scenarios.

![Flowchart for determining input to clustering algorithm](images/flowchart_od_potential_demand.png){#fig-flowchart-scenarios}

### Supply analysis {#sec-method-transport-supply}

A supply analysis is carried out to determine the OD pairs that are included in $OD_{s}$. The main components of transport supply are the road network, and the public transport timetables for buses and rail. We get the updated road network from OpenStreetMap. Bus timetable data is obtained in GTFS format from the Bus Open Data Service (BODS)[^2] and rail data is obtained from the Rail Delivery Group[^3].

[^2]: https://data.bus-data.dft.gov.uk/

[^3]: https://data.atoc.org/

The OSM road network and timetable data are fed into a multimodal routing engine [@pereira2021r5r] to calculate travel time between zones. Euclidean distance between an OD pair is used to calculate travel speed. OD pairs with speed below the 50th percentile or that require more than one transfer to be reached by public transport are considered to have poor supply.

### Demand analysis {#sec-method-transport-demand}

Our transport demand analysis is meant to identify bus routes that warrant an increase in route frequency. We calculate potential demand on all routes, and identify routes that have sufficient potential demand to warrant said increase in frequency. Potential demand is defined here as the demand along a bus route that could theoretically be served by the route (i.e. the route directly connects between the origin and destination zones). We only look at existing travel patterns and do not consider induced demand that could result from a better bus service.

To calculate potential demand on all routes, we do the following:

1.  *Determine which public transport routes directly serve each OD pair*: A route that directly serves an OD pair is a route that passes through both the origin and the destination zones associated with the OD pair. There can be multiple routes (common lines) serving each OD pair

2.  *Assign demand from OD pairs onto the bus routes*: Our flow data has trips for all MSOA pairs. We distribute demand from each OD pair onto its common lines (see @de2024modelling10 for overview of methods). We split the demand equally between common lines. Frequency-based assignment[^4] may better represent the status quo, but we chose to split the demand equally as our goal is to represent what the demand could be if route frequencies were improved.

3.  Get total potential demand on each route by summing the demand assigned from each OD pair

[^4]: Demand is distributed between the common lines (routes) in proportion to the frequency of each route

To determine which OD pairs to use in our analysis ($OD_{sd}$), we compare the potential demand on all routes. For each OD, we (a) get potential demand on all routes directly serving it. If potential demand on the busiest direct route serving OD \> 75th percentile of route demand, we do not include it in $OD_{sd}$ (see @fig-flowchart-scenarios).

OD pairs with high potential demand are not included in $OD_{sd}$ as there is sufficient demand to justify a high frequency bus route, even if one does not currently exist. The heuristic for calculating potential demand allows us to avoid serving areas with DRT just because there is poor public transport supply; there must also be insufficient demand to warrant a high frequency bus route.

Setting the threshold at $p75$ implies that service on the top 25% of routes in terms of potential demand will be improved so that they are all high-frequency routes. In reality, this % could be edited based on the budget available for additional buses.

## Clustering flow data {#sec-method-clustering-flow-data}

After filtering the OD trip data in the supply and demand analysis, we apply a spatial clustering approach to identify spatial concentrations in travel demand. Spatial statistics methods for cluster detection --- such as DBSCAN [@ester1996density] --- have mainly been developed for point data. Recently custom distance metrics that account for the multilocation nature of line data have allowed these methods to extend to flow data [@tao2016spatial].

We use the DBSCAN algorithm which takes two parameters: epsilon (the search radius to look for clusters) and minimum points (or minpts - the minimum number of points required to be inside the specified radius from a given point for a cluster to form around it). The distances between OD flows are the values that are compared to epsilon. It is calculated using the custom distance metric introduced by @tao2016spatial: let the flow process $F_{i}$ with origin $O_{i} (x_{i}, y_{i})$ and $D_{i} (u_{i}, v_{i})$ be modeled as a vector point with 4 coordinates $F_{i}(x_{i}, y_{i}, u_{i}, v_{i})$. The calculation for flow dissimilarity ($FDS_{ij}$) between $F_{i}$ and $F_{j}$ is shown in @eq-fds.

$$FDS_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha[(x_{i} - x_{j})^2 + (y_{i} - y_{j})^2] + \beta [(u_{i} - u_{j})^2 + (v_{i} - v_{j})^2]}{L_{i}L_{j}}}$$ {#eq-fds}

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ control the relative importance of the origins / destinations: higher $\alpha$ means we focus more on origins and vice-versa ($\alpha > 0$; $\beta > 0$; $\alpha + \beta = 2$). Dividing by the geometric mean of the flow lengths ($L_{i}$ and $L_{j}$ ) implies that, all else being equal, flow pairs of longer length are considered closer than shorter ones. A parameter sweep is done to determine feasible DBSCAN parameter combinations. A sensitivity analysis is then carried out to determine if minor changes to the parameters affect the clustering results.

## Clusters to potential DRT zones {#sec-methods-clusters-to-zones}

Our clustering algorithm may return clusters that cover large geographical areas. These areas may, in turn, be partly served by high frequency bus services. Having DRT cover the entirety of such areas may not be optimal as it (a) may provide competition to these bus services, and (b) may necessitate complex operations that make the service more prone to failure (as mentioned in @sec-lit-review).

We therefore propose a subsequent step to extract potential DRT zones from the obtained clusters. We get the spatial difference between each cluster and the high frequency bus routes in the study area (routes with at least 1 bus per hour), leaving us with polygons that extend to but do not overlap with said routes. This is in line with a DRT service that acts as a complimentary first/last mile connector.

# Results

In this section we present the clustering results for the morning peak period. As described in @sec-methods-preparing-data, the analysis was done for all time periods. @sec-results-transport-supply and @sec-results-transport-demand include the clustering results based on transport supply and transport supply + demand respectively. In the latter, we present more detailed examination of individual cluster composition. @sec-cluster-examination compares (a) how each cluster overlaps with different land-use classifications, (b) the number and length of the trips making up each cluster, and (c) the internal homogeneity of each cluster (in terms of the length and directionality of the trips make up the clusters). @sec-clusters-temporal shows the aggregate clustering results for different times of the day.

## Clustering based on transport supply only {#sec-results-transport-supply}

<!-- ![Connectivity of OD pairs](images/map_desire_commuting_facet_transfers.png){#fig-od-transfers-1 width="502"} -->

<!-- ![Connectivity of OD pairs (bar plot)](images/plot_bar_transfers_stacked_distance.png){#fig-od-transfers-2 width="300"} -->

@fig-cluster-scenario-2 and @fig-cluster-scenario-3 present the results of the clustering output of $OD_s$ and $OD_{sd}$ respectively. In these plots, each facet in the plot represents one of the main clusters produced by the DBSCAN algorithm. The components of the visual include:

a\) OD pairs: these are the straight lines with different colours. The different colours represent the number of trips represented by that OD pair. The endpoints of the OD pairs are also shown, with size corresponding to the number of trips.

b\) Cluster areas: Represented by the black dotted border, which is generated by getting the concave hull around the OD pairs in the cluster. The cluster area shows the spatial extent of the OD pairs that have been grouped together.

c\) Bus routes: High frequency bus routes are added as a background layer to give an overview of the current service. We use GTFS data (as mentioned in @sec-method-transport-supply) and keep only the routes operating at least 1 bus/hour in the morning peak

d\) Potential DRT zones: These are created by getting the spatial difference between the cluster areas and the bus routes. They visualise the areas in each cluster that are not served by a high frequency bus route, and the colours represent the sum of all trips in the OD pairs making up the cluster.

Examining the cluster areas (based on $OD_s$) in @fig-cluster-scenario-2, we see some geographical patterns in both the outskirts and closer to the urban core. We discuss these patterns by region:

-   **South and South West:** Clusters 8 and 10 represent trips connecting areas like Batley and Kirkhamgate to the urban core. These regions have poor public transport connections, with almost no high frequency bus routes extending from the centre all the way out there. Cluster 6 connects the South to a location slightly north of the urban core. The Southern area is not served by high frequency bus routes, and even the routes that extend to the South only connect to the city centre, and travellers are prone to long waiting times at the centre.

-   **West:** Clusters 3 and 9 show vertical travel demand from the North (e.g., Guiseley/Yeadon) and the South to Pudsey. These areas lack high frequency North-South public transport routes entirely, and public transport users are required to make a big detour into the centre to travel between them.

-   **North East:** Clusters 1 and 5 capture scattered travel demand between the rural North East and the urban core. There is only one high-frequency bus route extending to the North East, and trips that do not start or end near the only high frequency bus route do not have a viable public transport option. Even trips that do start or end near that route but do not end at the centre face potential long transfer times.

-   **North:** Cluster 2 includes rural areas with dispersed travel origins and limited public transport availability, with no routes extending to the Northern edges of the cluster. The cluster of the destinations slightly South of the urban core indicates that many of the trips with viable bus routes at their origin require a transfer at the centre.

-   **South East:** Cluster 7 shows concentrated travel demand from the South East to areas like Horsforth and neighbouring towns in the North West. These trips mostly originate in areas where no bus routes extend

The clustering analysis highlights several significant transport challenges across the study area.

1.  **PT not extending to the outskirts:** The clusters in the South and South West all connect to the city centre (8, 10, and 6). Even though PT services are mostly radial and into the city centre, these particular cases show the issue of PT services not extending far enough out to serve some travel demand in areas like Batley and Kirkhamgate. This seems to also be a factor in cluster 7, where there is no high frequency bus route extending to the South East.

2.  **Lack of North-South connectivity in West:** The vertical clusters in the West (3 and 9) underscore the absence of North-South public transport routes. While there is demand for travel between Pudsey and both towns like Guiseley/Yeadon in the North and Morley in the South, existing services primarily facilitate travel into the centre, leaving these trips unserved or requiring inefficient transfers. Cluster 4 is affected by the same issue, as most OD pairs probably do not fall along the bus route connecting the centre to the North West

3.  **Poor rural accessibility:** The North East clusters (1 and 5) and the rural North cluster (2) highlight challenges in providing transport to dispersed populations. Sparse travel demand and scattered origins/destinations make traditional fixed-route transport impractical. For trips to the urban core or other peripheral areas, there is only one high frequency route extending into the North East, and none into the North. The service area of these routes is only a small fraction of the area covered by the clusters.

4.  **Transfer time as part of cross-city travel**: Part of the unmet demand in the clusters could be due to long transfer times. This could be the case for cluster 7, which connects the South East to Horsforth in the North West. While some of the unmet demand is due to no high frequency bus routes extending into the South East, some origins in the South east that are along bus routes may suffer from long transfer times at the centre. Long transfer times could also explain part of the unmet demand in cluster 6.

These 4 challenges reveal gaps in the current public transport network, especially for rural areas in the outskirts and trips not going from/to the centre. DRT services could address these challenges by offering flexible, demand-responsive connections where high-frequency bus routes are impractical. This could take many forms, such as:

-   **DRT service to address entire trips:** DRT could serve as a standalone mode along the Western North-South axis, providing direct trips along the Guiseley/Yeadon-Pudsey axis in the North (Cluster 3), as well as the Morley-Pudsey axis in the South (Cluster 9).

-   **DRT as First/last-mile solution:** In sparsely populated areas like the North East and North (clusters 1, 2, and 5), DRT could act as a feeder service to high-frequency bus routes. By connecting dispersed travelers to high frequency bus routes, DRT enhances public transport accessibility and usability while maintaining the operational efficiency of the latter.

-   **DRT + improvements in PT headways / schedule synchronisation**: Clusters that cut through the city center may require a combination of DRT services and improvements in PT schedule synchronization. Cluster 2 and 6 are good examples of where DRT can offer a useful first/last mile service to connect to high frequency routes that go into the city center. However, given that these routes will not serve the entire trip in many cases, bus schedule synchronization in the city center will also be required to improve the passenger experience. These are examples of where a DRT service on its own is insufficient to create a viable PT offer.

Desire lines represent OD pairs making up each cluster, dashed black lines represent convex hull around desire lines, coloured polygons represent part of cluster that does not overlap with existing high frequency bus routes (see @sec-methods-clusters-to-zones)](images/map_clusters_scenario_2_equal_length_50000_bus_frac_grouped_gtfs_poly_lines_bus_diff_concave2_endpoints_crop.png){#fig-cluster-scenario-2 width="95%"}

## Clustering based on transport supply and demand {#sec-results-transport-demand}

In this section we look at the results of clustering OD pairs remaining after we do both the supply and demand analysis outlined in @fig-flowchart-scenarios ($OD_{sd}$). After comparing the results to those of $OD_s$ above, we further examine the cluster composition in @sec-cluster-examination, and then in in @sec-clusters-temporal we present the aggregate results from running the entire workflow for different points in time.

The clustering results are similar to those of $OD_s$ (presented in @sec-results-transport-supply), with some notable differences. Cluster 9 in @fig-cluster-scenario-3 appears to be a combination of cluster 8 and 10 in @fig-cluster-scenario-2. $OD_{sd}$ has fewer origin-destination pairs (@tbl-od_pairs_scenarios) as we exclude all OD pairs that have sufficient demand to warrant a bus service (see @sec-method-transport-demand). Our clustering algorithm finds clusters based on a minimum threshold of OD flows, and so fewer overall OD pairs means that a larger spatial coverage is required to obtain the same minimum threshold.

Another important difference is that cluster 5 in @fig-cluster-scenario-2 does not reappear here. Given the high demand from the urban core to the North East, the demand analysis (@sec-method-transport-demand) removed many of the OD pairs that were in that cluster, as they can be served by improved headway on existing public transport services. The remaining unserved OD pairs do not have enough concentrated demand to form a cluster on their own.

![Clustering results - OD pairs with poor PT supply and low potential demand ($OD_{sd}$) - Desire lines represent OD pairs making up each cluster, dashed black lines represent convex hull around desire lines, coloured polygons represent part of cluster that does not overlap with existing high frequency bus routes (see @sec-methods-clusters-to-zones)](images/map_clusters_scenario_3_equal_length_50000_bus_frac_grouped_gtfs_poly_lines_bus_diff_concave2_endpoints_crop.png){#fig-cluster-scenario-3 width="95%"}

### Examination of clusters {#sec-cluster-examination}

To better understand the clustering results, we analyse their spatial coverage, demand composition, and internal homogeneity (@fig-cluster-stats). This analysis helps assess (a) the effect of transforming clusters to DRT operating zones, (b) how well the clusters capture distinct patterns of travel demand, and (c) the differences in the number and length of the OD pairs making up each cluster.

In [@fig-cluster-stats-1] we see the urban/rural coverage of each cluster, both before and after removing areas that overlap with the high frequency bus network (step 3 in @fig-workflow). Comparing the original clusters to the extracted DRT operating zones, we see how the latter cover noticeably less urban areas than the former. This is because most of the urban core is served by high frequency bus routes. The operating zones are meant to connect to the high frequency bus network, and limiting the DRT service to the urban periphery is important for mitigating against DRT competition with public transport. The smaller service areas are easier to serve efficiently by a DRT fleet.

The clusters also vary in their composition, as shown in @fig-cluster-stats-2, which displays statistics for the OD pairs in each cluster. Some clusters are made up of many OD pairs each of which has a relatively small number of trips (e.g. cluster 8) whereas others have a few OD pairs with a large number of trips (e.g. cluster 3). The composition of the clusters (along with their spatial extent) can inform the type of DRT services [@d1994demand] to offer in each zone; a small number of high demand OD pairs could be served by a more direct service, whereas a cluster with many different, low demand OD pairs would be better served by a more flexible, many-to-many service. Clusters with a mix of high and low demand OD pairs may be better served by multiple DRT fleets with different operational characteristics.

@fig-cluster-stats-3 illustrates the internal homogeneity of OD flows in each cluster, focusing on the distribution of OD bearings and distances. Such homogeneity is key to our objective of capturing spatial concentrations of travel demand. Overall, we can see that most clusters have internal homogeneity in terms of OD bearings. Some clusters have highly concentrated demand, with most OD flows having very similar bearings and lengths (e.g. cluster 4 and 5). Other OD flows are more heterogeneous, with ODs of various lengths making up the cluster (e.g. cluster 1). For the more heterogeneous clusters, we still find that the majority of OD flows are inside one or two neighbouring distance brackets. For example, most OD flows in cluster 1 fall inside the 20-40km range. This is an indication that the clusters have some degree of homogeneity.

Noticeably, clusters made up of longer distance OD flows show more variance in their directionality, which can also be seen in @fig-cluster-scenario-3 (e.g. cluster 1 and 2). They tend to be anchored at one end and dispersed at the other. A couple of clusters (such as cluster 7) cover a significantly large spatial extent and their internal OD flows are not as concentrated. Shorter distance OD flows appear to have less circular variance and exhibit better concentration of demand at both endpoints. This is a result of our distance metric ([@eq-fds]) which normalizes distances by the length of the OD flows, thereby making longer flows appear closer than shorter ones.

### Aggregate result and temporal dimension {#sec-clusters-temporal}

In @fig-zones-one-map, we show how the potential DRT zones could look like if combined together. This includes merging all the cluster areas after step 3 in @fig-workflow. We show this for 5 times of day (described in @sec-methods-preparing-data) to show variation resulting from the combined effect of transport supply and travel demand changes throughout the data. The combined DRT zones all resemble similar doughnut shapes at the periphery of the study area, with the city centre being excluded due to the concentration of high frequency bus routes there. Combining cluster results into one map makes it even clearer that the potential DRT zones are predominantly in the outskirts and in areas with relatively low population densities. The doughnut shape is slightly bigger and more complete outside of the morning peak (12:30, 15:30, 18:30), and this can be explained by fewer bus services running during those times (fewer and thinner red lines).

![Aggregate DRT zones generated by combining individual DRT zones. Each facet shows the result for a different time of day. Although certain density-based clustering methods can work on arbitrarily shaped clusters of point process data (Pei et al. 2008), managing OD flow data is still difficult because shapes in OD flow space are arbitrary. # Discussion

In this paper, we propose a method for delineating DRT operating zones, addressing part of the need for strategic level methods that guide the design of DRT services. This is important as there is no well-defined methodology for identifying DRT service areas that effectively complement fixed-route public transport. Our proposed method is meant to inform strategic DRT planning and ensure integration with existing public transport services. As DRT evolves into a service that aims to improve accessibility for all, its integration with existing public transport services has become more important for offering multimodal alternatives to private car use [@nelson2010recent].

The success of DRT schemes is conditional on such integration and on their ability to serve spatial concentrations of travel demand [@enoch2006demand]. Using a density-based clustering algorithm, our analysis identified groups of OD flows with sufficiently similar patterns. This cluster identification can be used to design distinct DRT fleets based on the needs of each cluster (or group of similar clusters). Research has shown that assigning specific fleets to serve defined routes, rather than operating across the entire study area, improves system performance and fleet utilisation [@inturri2019multi]. This approach avoids the operational complexity that has historically undermined many DRT services [@enoch2006demand].

Our clustering results help highlight the different DRT services that could operate across our study area, Leeds. In areas such as the North-South axes in the West, DRT could serve as a standalone mode, providing direct trips where fixed-route public transport is unavailable. In sparsely populated rural areas in the periphery, DRT is better suited as a first/last-mile feeder service, connecting dispersed travellers to high-frequency public transport routes and thereby improving the accessibility and usability of the public transport system. Previous research has highlighted the potential of DRT feeders that extend bus services to rural areas [@sorensen2021much; @schluter2021impact]. However, DRT on its own is insufficient to improve the public transport offering in some cases. Clusters that traverse the city centre are made up of trips that may require a bus transfer, and the attractiveness of such trips largely depends on improvements in public transport headways and schedule synchronization.

The representation of the aggregated results at different times of day (@sec-clusters-temporal) demonstrates conceptually that a temporal dimension can be added to the analysis, and that temporal variations do exist. It is important to note that while there may be little temporal variation in these aggregated zones, this does not mean that the exact same services are required throughout the day. The disaggregate results (@fig-cluster-scenario-2 and @fig-cluster-scenario-3) are essential for understanding the variation in the specific clusters that make up each temporal snapshot. Such variation should inform the number of services and the operational characteristics of each service.

While we have used Leeds as a case study, the approach is generalisable to any city or region with an existing public transport network. The main requirements are public transport data (ideally in GTFS format) and travel demand matrices. We provide the code in a public repository[^5] to facilitate reproducibility and extension of the work.

[^5]: link to repository will be added if paper is accepted

## Implications for strategic planning of DRT

The composition and spatial extent of our clusters inform the design and operation of DRT services. Clusters vary in terms of the number and characteristics of OD pairs they encompass, supporting the evidence that DRT solutions need to be tailored to the area they are serving. Clusters with a high concentration of trips in a small area may require more direct services to one or two stops, while clusters with dispersed demand patterns may benefit from flexible, many-to-many DRT services.

Essential to our analysis is the use of DRT as part of an intermodal transport offering. It is clear that our clusters often overlap with high-frequency bus routes ([@fig-cluster-scenario-3]), highlighting the potential for DRT to act as a feeder service. By limiting DRT coverage to areas that are not covered by a high-frequency bus routes (step 3 in @fig-workflow), we aim to minimize unnecessary mode shift (e.g. public transport to DRT) and enhance the efficiency of public transport systems. Intermodal routing has only recently become possible in agent-based transport simulations [@haslebacher2018intermodal], with the integration of DRT into this intermodal framework being a subsequent development [@chouaki2023agent]. Such a framework should be used to test the feasibility of our DRT zones in facilitating intermodal trips, but it should be noted that the success of such integration is dependent on other factors besides operating zones, such as seamless transfers and fare structures that do not penalise the use of multiple modes.

The candidate zones identified by the method vary in size, and a follow up exercise would be necessary to validate them. Analytical models mentioned in @sec-planning_drt could be used to determine more precise service areas. They could identify whether the critical demand density for a DRT service is met [@quadrifoglio2009methodology], look at schedule coordination with bus network [@sivakumaran2012cost], and predict DRT performance based on the street network layout in the different zones [@chandra2013new]. Future work could also explore optimisation approaches --- such as extensions to the Transit Network Design and Frequency Setting Problem (TNDFSP) --- that can output both a bus network and DRT service areas.

<!--# Simulations are necessary to inform which solution is more suitable. Discrete event simulations (citation) can be used to inform DRT efficiency under different operating characteristics. More sophisticated agent-based models could help us understand how -->

## Comparison with alternative methods

Alternative methods have been used to identify DRT operating areas. One approach is to focus on the supply side, and allow DRT to operate in areas of poor public transport accessibility [@giuffrida2021addressing; @rath2023assessing]. While such extensive service provision is important from a transport equity perspective, the lack of focus on demand could lead to DRT services with low passenger load factors [@creutzig2024shared]. Areas with poor accessibility are also normally spread out across a study area, and it is important to go beyond just identifying these areas to seeing how they can be grouped into similar demand patterns so as not to operate overly complex DRT services that cannot pool travel demand [@enoch2006demand].

Optimization models typically start with an existing public transport network and focus on incremental adjustments, such as modifying route frequencies, removing or trimming routes, or adjusting DRT fleet sizes [@pinto2020joint; @zhao2021joint]. While valuable for fine-tuning service operations, these models either allow DRT to operate across the entire network, or limit service areas to the edges of existing bus routes. A more flexible approach to service area delineation, informed by demand patterns, could serve as either a simpler alternative to complex optimization models or as a way to define initial DRT service areas for further refinement through optimization.

## Limitations and future work

### Input data and demand analysis

In the approach outlined in this paper, we conduct a supply and demand analysis to ensure that we focus only on OD flows that are not, or do not have the necessary demand to be, served by a high frequency bus route. Our demand analysis is based on splitting OD demand equally between its common lines. While this is justified by our need to represent route demand given hypothetical improvements in headway, more robust methods can be used for scenario modelling of such improvements. Our results can be used as input for an optimisation frameworks that adjust route headways and DRT fleet sizes, given pre-defined DRT service areas [@pinto2020joint]. They could also be used as an initial solution for optimisation frameworks that simultaneously modify public transport routes and DRT service areas [@zhao2021joint]. Since the core novelty of our approach is the identification of spatial concentrations in travel demand, we deliberately avoid adding further layers of complexity. This allows the results to be useful as an output in themselves, or as input to optimisation and agent-based simulation frameworks for further refinements.

Moreover, our current method is based on trip matrices at MSOA level with little information besides number of people. Datasets that have complete travel patterns of a population, such as activity-based models [@rasouli2014activity] would give us a more representative picture of travel demand and trip chains throughout the day. They would also enable linking travel patterns to sociodemographic characteristics and analysing for which categories of people and trip purposes DRT can improve accessibility.

### Refinements to clustering algorithm

The clustering algorithm used (DBSCAN) requires the input of two parameters: epsilon (the search radius) and minpts (the minimum number of points inside the radius necessary for a cluster to form). In the absence of established theoretical framework for this approach, we adopt an iterative and exploratory method to parameter setting. Future work could explore algorithms that simultaneously identify clusters at different scales [@tao2017flowhdbscan; @fang2021adaptive] to avoid having results based on one fixed radius.

<!--# Additionally, different density-based clustering algorithms such as HDBSCAN [@tao2017flowhdbscan] and OPTICS [@fang2021adaptive] can also be explored. Both of these algorithms require only one input parameter and can identify cluster formation at different scales. Identifying clusters at different scales can provide results that are well–suited to variations in population density and can also allow researchers and practitioners to compare different options for the same area. -->

Another component of the clustering algorithm worth exploring further is the metric used to calculate distance between flows. Our clustering algorithm relies on distances between OD flows when creating clusters. Given the large study area, and the variation in trip distances, we use a distance metric [@tao2016spatial] that normalizes distances so that the values cover a smaller range. This is useful for DBSCAN, which takes one value for the search radius. If we do not normalize the flows, our distance metric will have a wider range, but we would not be able to choose a search radius that accommodates all the flows (a smaller radius would produce better results for shorter flows, and a larger search radius would produce distorted clusters that group the shorter flows with the longer ones). However, this normalization is not perfect, as can be seen in @fig-cluster-stats-3 where some clusters have OD flows of various lengths. To overcome the issue of scale associated with OD flows of various lengths, the following research directions could be explored:

-   *Improvements to the current distance metric*: Consider other approaches to flow normalization such as transformations to the denominator that reduce the effect of the OD length (e.g. log transformations). Additionally, a parameter that explicitly represents OD flow bearing may help reduce circular variance inside each cluster. <!--# Another improvement could be to put a higher weight on the $\alpha$ or $\beta$ parameters to focus on identifying clusters of trip start and end points that share a roughly similar trip direction. Given our emphasis on linking the outskirts to the urban core, focusing on endpoints could pool more OD pairs and give us areas that should be served by a last-mile service $\alpha$ -->

-   *Using different distance metrics*: Metrics such as Fréchet distance [@eiter1994computing] could be used. The Fréchet distance measures curve similarity by determining minimum "leash" length needed to traverse both curves simultaneously.

-   *Clustering at different scales*: Instead of editing or changing the distance metric, we could try clustering at different scales. This could be done by partitioning the data by length and running DBSCAN separately for each subgroup, or by using different density-based clustering algorithms such as HDBSCAN [@tao2017flowhdbscan] and OPTICS [@fang2021adaptive]. Both of these algorithms can identify cluster formation at different scales, allowing us to extract clusters of different lengths without worrying about distance normalization in our distance metric.

<!--# Identifying clusters at different scales can provide results that are well–suited to variations in population density -->

# Conclusion

The need to decarbonise the transport sector, improvements in real-time routing technology, and the proliferation of app-based services have all contributed to a surge in DRT research and real-world schemes [@castellanos2022technology]. However DRT services continue to suffer from the lack of robust strategic level planning, and many fail to capture sufficient passenger demand to make them economically viable [@enoch2006demand; @creutzig2024shared]. The OD clustering approach presented in this paper addresses these challenges by identifying potential DRT operating zones based on spatial concentrations of unmet travel demand, making them more likely to be viable and effective in reducing car dependency.

Strategic planning of DRT that accounts for its integration with more traditional public transport systems presents a promising avenue for improved mobility in areas with pockets of concentrated travel demand that are difficult to serve cost-effectively by fixed-route public transport. The approach presented in this paper offers both conceptual and methodological contributions that can help realise this promise. Conceptually, we borrow methods from spatial data mining and argue that they are well suited to filling gaps in the current approaches for strategic planning of DRT services. We build on this concept methodologically by embedding a clustering algorithm into a larger transport planning pipeline with more traditional supply and demand components. Our findings show that spatial clustering of OD flow data can contribute to delineating operating zones in strategic DRT planning, but that more research should be done on improving distance metrics that are core to clustering and on refining the supply and demand analysis used to extract the OD flows to be clustered.

The approach can be adopted by practitioners in early stage strategic planning of DRT, and the outputs can be tested in agent-based simulations to understand how a service could perform in one of the suggested zones, the operational characteristics required, and the associated mode shift and VMT on the network under different scenarios.
